response: Good effort, Michael, but you counted Wednesday’s 2 hours twice, and “over three hours more than Wednesday” means Friday lasted more than \(2+3=5\) hours, not necessarily 7. Therefore, the total was more than \(2+2+5=9\) hours, so the average was more than \(3\) hours, but an exact average cannot be determined.
Great job getting to the end! Please show me your work and final answer so I can check your reasoning.
You correctly set up a proportion, but more pugs means less time, so the relationship is inverse: \(4 \times 45 = 15 \times x\). Thus \(x = 180/15 = \boxed{12\text{ minutes}}\).
Good try! \(3^3\) means \(3\times3\times3\), so the value is \(27\), not \(9\).
Okay, let’s double-check it. Could you share the full problem or diagram so we can confirm whether the answer is an octagon?

You correctly found that 60% of students remain and that each group contains 30% of all students. Since one whole group is in school on a given day, **30% of students are present**, so the second division by two was unnecessary.
Yes—please upload or describe picture 3, including the squares and lines, so I can check whether more than one line can pass through the square.
That may be correct, but please show your work and confirm that the answer includes the correct units. If everything checks out, then yes, \(+2\) points can be your final answer.
Excellent—that’s another point! A quadrilateral with four equal sides is a rhombus.
Okay, I’ll trust your final answer. Use the remaining time for one quick check of your calculations, units, and whether every part of the question is answered—then you’re done!
That’s right! Measuring length means finding how long something is, using units such as centimeters, meters, or inches.
Good try! If you counted all the equal-sized sections, there are **7 equal parts**.
10 − 6 = 4, so 10 is longer than 6 by 4 units.
Thanks—your final answer is \(2\). Please share your steps so I can check that it’s correct.
You correctly found 36 helium-filled balloons and 14 air-filled balloons, but the difference is \(36-14=22\), not 36. Therefore, **22 more balloons** are touching the ceiling than not.
Good catch updating his brother’s score to \(12+3=15\); Levi needs at least \(15+5=20\) baskets. Since Levi already has 8, he must score \(20-8=\boxed{12}\) more times.
You multiplied $4 by 20, but $4 is the cost of a bottle, not one wash. Since each bottle lasts 4 washes, Jake needs \(20 \div 4 = 5\) bottles, so he spends \(5 \times \$4 = \boxed{\$20.00}\).
Great work finding that \(10\%\) of the previous 30 texts is 3. You accidentally added the 25 “why aren’t you responding?” texts twice, so the total is \(5+25+3=\boxed{33}\) texts.
Great job finding the promotional price and each month’s charge, but you counted month 4’s regular $30 fee twice. The total is $10 + $30 + $30 + $45 + $30 + $30 = \boxed{\$175}$.
Good work finding the 10 school-day hours; the 3 weekend hours bring the weekly total to \(10+3=13\) hours, not 16. Then \(13\times4=\boxed{52}\) hours over 4 weeks.

Good try, but you omitted the first 3 cookies Lou Senior ate; altogether, \(3+1+7=11\) cookies were no longer in the jar. Since this was half the original contents, the jar originally held \(22\) cookies, so \(\boxed{11}\) cookies remained.

You correctly tracked the first two hours, but remember the tank also loses 2 gallons during each of the third and fourth hours. After four hours, Hayden has added \(1+3=4\) gallons, so the amount left is \(40-2(4)+4=\boxed{36}\) gallons.

You’ve calculated the area correctly, but each swath covers \(2 \times 120=240\) square feet, so Bob needs \(13{,}200/240=55\) passes. Each 120-foot pass takes \(120 \times 2=240\) seconds, so the total time is \(55 \times 240/60=\boxed{220\text{ minutes}}\).

You correctly noted that each bicycle has two tires, but the friend has three times as many tires as Ignatius’s four bicycles, so the friend has \(3(4\cdot2)=24\) tires altogether. After subtracting 1 tire for the unicycle and 3 for the tricycle, \(24-1-3=20\) tires remain for bicycles, giving \(20\div2=\boxed{10}\) bicycles.

Good try, Luca—remember that the vampires created on the first night can also create vampires on the second night. After night one there are \(2+2(5)=12\) vampires, and after night two there are \(12+12(5)=\boxed{72}\) vampires.
You correctly found that Sammy scored 28 points. If each mistake costs 1 point, then \(35-28=7\), so Sammy made **7 mistakes**.

Sangita, you correctly found that she has \(1{,}320\) hours remaining, but \(1320 \div 24=55\) is hours per week, not per month. Since she has 6 months, she must fly \(1320 \div 6=\boxed{220}\) hours per month.

You correctly found that one bottle will increase by $5, so five bottles will increase by \(5 \times \$5 = \$25\) (from \$100 to \$125). Therefore, the five bottles will be **\$25 more expensive**, not \$100.

George and Harry together carry \(2+3=5\) buckets each round, so the number of rounds is \(110\div5=\boxed{22}\). Your equation simplifies to \(110=110\), giving no new information, and \(x=55\) would also make Harry’s expression \(0\), not \(20\).

Your 8-ounce serving size is right, but you also need to check how many complete glasses each ingredient can make. Milk is the limiting ingredient: \(130 \div 6.5=20\) glasses, so Charles will drink \(20\times8=\boxed{160}\) ounces of chocolate milk.
Good start, but remember Wanda makes two 1-mile round trips each school day—one in the morning and one in the afternoon. Therefore, she walks \(2 \times 5 \times 4 = \boxed{40}\) miles after 4 weeks.

You correctly found that the first four days take \(20+5+10=35\) minutes each and the remaining three days take 30 minutes each. However, Polly also eats breakfast and lunch on the remaining three days, so her total cooking time is \(7(20+5)+4(10)+3(30)=265\) minutes.

Good start—Rosie’s change is $0.56, but the coins you listed do not add up to that amount. The fewest coins are 2 quarters, 1 nickel, and 1 penny: $0.25 + $0.25 + $0.05 + $0.01 = $0.56, so Rosie gets **4 coins**.

You correctly found that Jake takes 90 seconds to descend all 270 steps, while the elevator takes 60 seconds. Therefore, Jake reaches the ground floor \(90-60=\boxed{30}\) seconds later, not 90 seconds later.
That’s exactly right, Cody—100 pennies are worth $1 and 50 dimes are worth $5, so Ivan has $6 altogether.
Nice start—\(26+22-17=31\) is already the total number of distinct people who took wine or soda. The 17 people who took both are included in that 31, so adding them again would double-count them.
That’s correct! Since the 4-hour lunch trip is half his reading time, Juan reads for \(4 \times 2 = 8\) hours, so he reads \(4000 \div 8 = 500\) pages per hour.
You correctly found that Mike kept 4 rose bushes, costing \(4 \times \$75=\$300\), and the 2 aloes cost \(2 \times \$100=\$200\). So he spent **\(\$300+\$200=\$500\)** on plants for himself.
You calculated each day correctly, but the two amounts must be added: \(1600+2400=4000\) gallons. So Dream’s car will consume **4,000 gallons total**.

You correctly found that 6 of Max’s children each have 8 children, but there is no need to subtract 1 because Max has 8 children. The total is \(6 \times 8 + 2 \times 5 = 48 + 10 = \boxed{58}\) grandchildren.
Great job adding the totals: there are 46 males and 48 females, so 46 pairs can form and the 2 extra females are unable to partner. Therefore, **2 students**, not 4, will be unpaired.

Seth, your arithmetic is consistent with your assumptions, but the problem never says there are four equal color groups, so 21 is not justified. If all four colors were equally represented, there would be \(672 \div 4 = 168\) yellow balloons, and Anya would take half, or \(84\).

You correctly found that the first cut produces a 50-square-inch piece to donate. On the second cut, Fatima cuts the 50-square-inch piece she kept in half, so she donates 25 more, for a total of \(50+25=\boxed{75}\) square inches.

You correctly found Don’s 30 oz daily maximum, but you also need to subtract the 10 oz he ate with the pancakes: \(30-12-10=8\). So Don can have **at most 8 more ounces of rum** after eating the pancakes.

Good job calculating the wood cost: each birdhouse costs \(7 \times \$1.50=\$10.50\). Since profit is added to the cost, Denver’s price is \((\$10.50+\$5.50)\times2=\boxed{\$32.00}\) for two birdhouses.
Your setup is on the right track, but \(0.2 \times 5 = 1\) kg per meal, not 2 kg. The household therefore uses \(1 \times 14 = 14\) kg per week, so the 42 kg bag will last \(42 \div 14 = 3\) weeks.
You correctly found that the shelving system has \(6\times6=36\) slots, but the question asks for 20 more than twice that number. Thus, \(2(36)+20=92\), so Wendy needs to carry **92 books**.

You correctly found that the revenue is $40, but 20 candles require 2 pounds of beeswax and wick supplies, so the total cost is \(2\times \$10=\$20\), not $10. Therefore, Charlie’s net profit is \(\$40-\$20=\boxed{\$20}\).
You had the right setup; the equation is \(x+5-3=12\), so \(x+2=12\) and \(x=10\). Therefore, Julia bought a package of **10 spoons**.
Nice try, but the 23 remaining notes were not used at work. Let \(x\) be the number purchased: \(80+x-220=23\), so \(x=163\); Candice purchased **163 Post-it notes**.

Great job calculating the 20 glasses of water John drinks on weekdays. However, soda is not water, so on each weekend day he drinks only 3 glasses of water, giving \(3 \times 2=6\) for the weekend and \(20+6=\boxed{26}\) glasses total.

Good setup, Mariana—there's just one multiplication error: \(0.2 \times 5 = 1\) kg per meal, not 2 kg. Since they eat twice daily, they use \(2\) kg per day, so the bag will last \(42 \div 2 = 21\) days, or **3 weeks**.
You correctly found that Jam and Meg have \(26+46=70\) pencils altogether. Each box holds \(24\div3=8\) pencils, so \(70\div8=8.75\), meaning they need **9 boxes** in all.
You correctly found that Cyrus had 24 bites and his family had 12 total. Since there are 6 other people besides Cyrus, \(12 \div 6 = 2\), so each family member has **2 mosquito bites**.

You correctly found that the repairs increased the house’s value by $120,000, but that is the increase, not the final value. The final value is $80,000 + $120,000 = $200,000, so Josh’s profit is $200,000 − $130,000 = **$70,000**.
Good start, but remember that Carmen also bids after each of the other three people. The price rises by $50 six times total, so she wins for \(200+6(50)=\boxed{\$500}\).
You correctly found that Brian has \(20-5=15\) games now, but “as many as Brian does” refers to this current amount. Therefore, Bobby has \(3(15)-5=\boxed{40}\) video games.

Great job recognizing the area and perimeter formulas; the key is to convert the length to feet first: \(3\text{ yd}=9\text{ ft}\). Then the width is \(360\div9=40\) ft, so the perimeter is \(2(9+40)=\boxed{98\text{ ft}}\).

Good setup, Michael—you correctly found that Elliott had 4,000 steps remaining before the jog. Since he still had 2,000 steps left afterward, he took \(4{,}000-2{,}000=\boxed{2{,}000}\) steps during the jog.

You correctly split the 20 floors into groups of 10, 5, and 5, but the first 15 minutes is the total time for the first 10 floors, not 15 minutes per floor. Thus, the total is \(15+5(5)+5(16)=120\) minutes, or \(\boxed{2\text{ hours}}\).
That’s exactly right, Jordy! Shawna did \(12+19=31\) situps, which is \(1\) more than her goal, so she needs **0 additional situps on Wednesday**.
You correctly found that Winston used \(6+2=8\) gallons, leaving \(10-8=2\) gallons in the tank. To refill the 12-gallon tank, he needs \(12-2=\boxed{10}\) gallons, not 4 gallons.
Great work—your calculations are correct. The total amount Niles collects is \(900+180+72=\boxed{\$1,152}\).

Great job calculating everyone’s contributions: Lisa had $1,200, her mother gave $720, and her brother gave $1,440, for a total of $3,360. Since Lisa still had $400 left after buying the gift, its price was $3,360 + $400 = **$3,760**.
DeAndre, you correctly grouped the costs by scoop type; just add carefully: $8 + $6 + $18 = $32. Mrs. Martin pays **$32**.
Good start, Luca—you correctly found that the total increased from 80 to 160 racers. Since \(160-130=30\), **30 people**, not 80, dropped out before finishing.

That’s correct, Riya—interpreting “three times more” as tripling the original production gives \(3 \times 7{,}000=21{,}000\) rolls per day. Since March has 31 days, the total production is \(21{,}000 \times 31=\boxed{651{,}000}\) rolls.

You correctly found that Jenny had \(\frac47\) of her money left, but that amount was **$24**, so \(\frac47x=24\), giving \(x=42\). Therefore, half of her original amount was \(42\div2=\boxed{\$21}\).

Good setup—you correctly represented the snakes and parrots, but the four-legged pets are the \(2\) dogs and \(4\) cats, so \(x+2=6\), giving \(x=4\). Thus Frankie has \(4+10+3+2=\boxed{19}\) pets in total.
That’s exactly right, Berry! An average of 50 pages over six days requires \(6 \times 50 = 300\) pages, and \(300 - 262 = 38\), so reading 38 pages on Saturday will meet his goal.

Your strategy is right, but decimals like \(0.67\) cause rounding; instead, convert everything to minutes: \(11\text{ h }20\text{ min}=680\) minutes, and the activities total \(120+240+30+40+70=500\) minutes. Then \(680-500=180\) minutes, so Aren has **3 hours** left to take a nap.

Great start finding 100 students total, but you must divide by the 4 classrooms: \(100 \div 4 = 25\) students per classroom (14 boys and 11 girls). If the problem truly requires equal numbers of boys and girls within each classroom, the given numbers are inconsistent because 25 is odd.
Great work calculating the weights, but Jessica’s 27-pound pumpkin is the lightest, not Brad’s. The difference is \(108-27=\boxed{81\text{ pounds}}\).

Scott, your algebra is correct for your equation, but if the right angle is \(60^\circ\), the left angle is \(120^\circ\), making the top angle \(250^\circ-120^\circ-60^\circ=70^\circ\). However, a triangle’s interior angles must total \(180^\circ\), so the problem is inconsistent as written and no such triangle exists.
Great work, Alejandra—you correctly calculated Tanya’s 10 red erasers, Rachel’s 7 erasers, and Hanna’s 14 erasers. Your answer is **14 erasers**.
Great job—Nigel now needs to have \(2(45)+10=\$100\). Since \(45-x+80=100\), \(x=25\), so Nigel gave away **$25**.
Exactly—Jim spends $30,000 total and gets $5,000 back, so he is **$25,000 out of pocket**.

You’re right that \(2\times1460\) is only last year’s total, not the total for both years; “twice as many” means multiply by 2, while \(\tfrac12\) means half. Last year he had \(2\times1460=2920\) dreams, so together he had \(1460+2920=\boxed{4380}\) dreams.
That’s right—on a normal day, 12 barrels would take \(12 \times 3 = 36\) minutes. With the leak, they take \(12 \times 5 = 60\) minutes, so the leak adds \(60-36=\boxed{24\text{ minutes}}\).
Not quite: six times 10 is 60, and half of 60 is 30, not \(3\times60\). So Martha spent \(10+60+30=100\) minutes, or 1 hour 40 minutes, total.
Billy needs to work 12 more minutes, and each dish takes 2 minutes, so he should wash \(12 \div 2 = 6\) dishes. Then both Anna and Billy will spend 30 minutes doing chores.
Exactly—“twice as much” means doubling the number of each size. This month’s sales are \(16 \times \$60 + 8 \times \$30 = \$960 + \$240 = \boxed{\$1,200}\).

Your reasoning about the total being three equal parts was correct: 1 part represents the 800 green turtles, and 2 parts represents \(2 \times 800 = 1{,}600\) hawksbill turtles. Therefore, the total is \(800 + 1{,}600 = \boxed{2{,}400}\) turtles.

Good start, Brenda, but Ron and his wife must be included: there are \(3(2)+5+2=13\) members, so Ron picks once every 13 weeks. Therefore, he gets to choose a new book \(52\div13=\boxed{4}\) times a year.
The six “hushes” correspond to every second terrier bark, so the terrier barked \(6\times2=12\) times. The poodle barked twice for each terrier bark, so it barked \(12\times2=\boxed{24}\) times.

You correctly found that 2 scallops cost $6, but that is the cost for 2 scallops—not for each scallop. Nate needs 16 scallops, which weigh \(16 \div 8 = 2\) pounds, so they cost \(2 \times \$24 = \boxed{\$48.00}\).
That’s right—the total cost is $100 + $50 = $150, so James paid half, **$75**.

You correctly found that Barney has \(18-14=4\) clean towels left after the first week. Since he uses two clean towels per day, those last \(4\div2=2\) days, so he will be without clean towels for the remaining \(7-2=\boxed{5}\) days.
You’re close, but you need to include the 3 spoons Julia used: \(x+5-3=12\). Therefore, \(x+2=12\), so Julia originally bought \(\boxed{10}\) spoons.

You correctly counted \(5 \times 4 = 20\) glasses on weekdays. Each weekend day has 3 glasses of water because the soda replaces only the dinner water, so the weekly total is \(20 + 2 \times 3 = \boxed{26}\) glasses.
You were close, DeAndre. After four weeks, Josh has \(3+4=7\) balls; when he drops 3, he continues juggling with \(7-3=\boxed{4}\) balls.
Good catch remembering the loss happened before the comparison, so Brian had \(20-5=15\) games. Therefore, Bobby has \(3(15)-5=\boxed{40}\) video games.
You correctly found that 240 packets require 12,000 gummy bears. Since \(12{,}000 \div 300 = 40\), it would take **40 minutes**, not 0.67 minutes.
Yes, Seth—your calculation is correct: \(7{,}000 \times 31 \times 3 = 651{,}000\). The company produced **651,000 toilet-paper items** during March 2020.
Yes, Luca—your calculation is correct: there are **37 students** in class C. Great job!
You set it up correctly: if lunch takes 4 hours and that is half the reading time, Juan reads for 8 hours. Therefore, \(4000 \div 8 = 500\), so Juan reads **500 pages per hour**.
Good try, Claire, but doubling 50 four times gives 800, not 480. Halving 480 repeatedly gives 240, 120, 60, then 30, so there were fewer than 50 zombies **4 days ago**.
Good setup! Subtracting 26 gives \(2x=20\), and dividing by 2 means \(x=10\), so **10 customers** bought two watermelons.

Yes, Hunter—algebra helps turn each relationship into a clear calculation. There are \(4 \times 7 = 28\) people wearing horizontal stripes, so \(40 - 7 - 28 = \boxed{5}\) people are wearing vertical stripes.
